conflicts.point: Whether upstream physical infrastructure controls, such as extreme ultraviolet lithography and gigawatt-scale grid telemetry, can effectively prevent the proliferation of frontier AI models without creating regulatory monopolies.

positions.stance: Upstream physical hardware controls and real-time grid telemetry provide an auditable, enforceable chokepoint that governs frontier R&D without creating prohibitive compliance burdens for smaller entities.
Upstream hardware rationing and monitoring mechanisms function as bureaucratic monopolies that protect incumbent firms and fail to prevent distributed compute circumvention.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream physical infrastructure controls can effectively prevent the proliferation of frontier AI models without creating regulatory monopolies.
verdicts.rationale: Both sides present valid systemic risks that neither model fully resolves. The safety position correctly identifies physical chokepoints like extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, but underestimates the difficulty of preventing decentralized, peer-to-peer compute networks from training smaller yet dangerous weights. Conversely, the accelerationist position highlights documented lobbying expenditures by large technology firms, but offers no empirical mechanism to prevent the proliferation of dangerous frontier models once open-source weights are widely distributed.
